issues.subcategory: Novelty claim in the Abstract feels too broad
issues.description: Novelty claim in the Abstract feels too broad: The Abstract's broad statement that little is known about the relationship between spelling and meaning in alphabetic writing systems appears somewhat overstated relative to the introduction's own review of substantial work on morphological regularities in printed words. The gap seems narrower: the corpus-scale quantification of suffix spelling-to-lexical-category mappings, and whether skilled readers' behaviour tracks those graded mappings.
issues.quote: Substantial research has been undertaken to understand the relationship between spelling and sound, but we know little about the relationship between spelling and meaning in alphabetic writing systems. We present a computational analysis of English writing in which we develop new constructs to describe this relationship. Diagnosticity captures the amount of meaningful information in a given spelling, whereas specificity estimates the degree of dispersion of this meaning across different spellings for a particular sound sequence.

issues.subcategory: Specificity definition in the Abstract is directionally unclear
issues.description: Specificity definition in the Abstract is directionally unclear: The Abstract's description of specificity as the 'degree of dispersion' is directionally unclear. Later, high specificity means that a lexical-category function for a given sound sequence is concentrated in, or preferentially realised by, a particular spelling; if that function were dispersed across many spellings, the specificity value for any one spelling would be lower.
issues.quote: Diagnosticity captures the amount of meaningful information in a given spelling, whereas specificity estimates the degree of dispersion of this meaning across different spellings for a particular sound sequence. Using these two constructs, we demonstrate that particular suffix spellings tend to be reserved for particular meaningful functions.

issues.subcategory: Methodological contradiction in describing Farmer et al.
issues.description: Methodological contradiction in describing Farmer et al.: The description of Farmer et al. (2006) is internally inconsistent: a self-paced reading methodology normally yields reading-time measures, whereas 'read aloud faster' suggests an oral reading or naming latency. The phrase therefore appears to misstate the dependent measure in this background example.
issues.quote: using a self-paced reading methodology, Farmer et al. (2006) found that when sentence context generated an expectation for a noun, phonologically-typical nouns (e.g. marble whose phonological features cluster with those of other nouns) were read aloud faster than phonologically-atypical nouns (e.g. insect whose phonological features cluster with those of verbs).

issues.subcategory: Questionable example of orthographic and semantic overlap
issues.description: Questionable example of orthographic and semantic overlap: The example 'sneeze-SNORE' may not be the clearest illustration of combined orthographic and semantic overlap, since its formal overlap is limited mainly to the initial 'sn-' sequence. The broader point may still be right, but this example can read as weaker evidence against a simple orthographic-plus-semantic account than the surrounding comparison suggests.
issues.quote: It is noteworthy that this priming effect cannot be ascribed to simple orthographic overlap between prime and target (e.g. brothel-BROTH where -EL is not an existing morpheme yields no priming; Rastle et al., 2004), or the simple summation of orthographic and semantic overlap (e.g. sneeze-SNORE yields no priming; Rastle et al., 2000).

issues.subcategory: Phonological confusion regarding the suffix -ED
issues.description: Phonological confusion regarding the suffix -ED: The -ED illustration appears to mix orthographic and phonological levels. The passage frames the relevant comparison around the word-final sound sequence $/\varepsilon \mathrm{d}/$, but regular past-tense -ED is normally realised as /t/, /d/, or syllabic /ɪd/~/əd/, not /ɛd/. The examples also do not all match the stated sequence: naked and wicked normally end in /ɪd/ or /əd/. This is a local problem in the motivating example rather than an apparent issue for the paper’s derivational-suffix analyses.
issues.quote:
Similar dependency characterizes English inflectional suffixes. For example, it is well known that spelling -ED is
strongly indicative of past tense (e.g. Carney, 1994). However, it has only recently come to light that the word-final sound sequence $/ \varepsilon \mathrm{d} /$ in morphologically-simple words is typically spelled in a different manner (e.g. instead; Berg et al., 2014). In fact, there are only a handful of morphologically-simple words ending in this sound sequence spelled -ED that could potentially be treated as comprising more than one morpheme (e.g. biped, moped, naked, wicked; Berg et al., 2014).

issues.subcategory: Speech-writing analogy points in the opposite direction
issues.description: Speech-writing analogy points in the opposite direction: The -ED example says writing preserves a cue more clearly than speech. Intonation and emphasis are examples of the reverse: information preserved in speech but often weakened or lost in writing. “Just like” therefore misleads the reader. Recast the sentence as a contrast rather than a parallel.
issues.quote: Thus, the relationship between form and meaning in this instance appears to be stronger in written language than in spoken language - just like other types of meaningful information are preserved in speech, but lost in writing (e.g. intonation, emphasis; Seidenberg, 2017).

issues.subcategory: Jabberwocky example does not isolate the -AL cue
issues.description: Jabberwocky example does not isolate the -AL cue: The preceding sentence establishes that -AL cues adjective-or-noun status more than verb status, not adjective status alone. In “vorpal blade”, the pre-nominal position already tells the reader that the nonce word is functioning as a modifier. If the example stays, present -AL as reinforcing a category interpretation supplied by the syntax rather than as isolating the adjective cue by itself.
issues.quote: For example, the spelling -AL communicates adjective or noun status (i.e. not a verb), and adjectives ending in the sound sequence /əl/ are most likely spelled -AL. Might these observations help us to understand why Lewis Carroll (1871/1983) chose the spelling "vorpal" as opposed to "vorple" to describe the young hero's blade in Jabberwocky?

issues.subcategory: Co-variation does not by itself dichotomise the suffix space
issues.description: Co-variation does not by itself dichotomise the suffix space: Co-variation among graded measures does not automatically produce two categories. Even perfect co-variation could give a continuum, such as D = S = 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8. A dichotomy would require a thresholding rule or evidence for two separated clusters. A better formulation is that strong co-variation might make a single graded measure sufficient.
issues.quote: It is a valid theoretical possibility that diagnosticity and specificity always co-vary thus dichotomising the English derivational space into two categories (diagnostic and specific vs not diagnostic and not specific).

issues.subcategory: Inaccurate parenthetical definition of specificity
issues.description: Inaccurate parenthetical definition of specificity: The parenthetical gloss of specificity as “probability of a cue given a category” is incomplete. Because specificity is defined elsewhere relative to a given sound sequence and competing spellings, the intended quantity is closer to $P(\text{spelling cue} \mid \text{category}, \text{sound sequence})$; without that conditioning, the gloss describes a different and broader measure.
issues.quote: Here we hypothesise that the bidirectional relationship between the form and the meaning cannot be captured using a unitary concept (e.g. cue validity), and needs to be expressed through the combination of diagnosticity and specificity (probability of a cue given a category).

issues.subcategory: Most-frequent-pronunciation rule needs its consequence stated
issues.description: Most-frequent-pronunciation rule needs its consequence stated: Because specificity is conditioned on a sound sequence, this choice narrows the interpretation of the specificity values. Some suffix spellings have category-linked pronunciations, so the non-selected pronunciations may not be described by the reported specificity estimate. Add a sentence saying that specificity values refer only to the most frequent pronunciation of each suffix spelling, and clarify how uses with other pronunciations were treated.
issues.quote: The number of words extracted for each suffix is presented in Appendix A. Our analyses consider three major lexical categories: nouns, adjectives, and verbs. Only the most frequent pronunciation was considered for each suffix.

issues.subcategory: Diagnosticity denominator in the Method section
issues.description: Diagnosticity denominator in the Method section: The type diagnosticity definition appears to use the wrong denominator. As written, it describes $P(\text{suffix} \mid \text{category})$, but the conceptual definition, examples (-TUDE = 1; -IAN = 0.54), token formula, and Appendix A values indicate that diagnosticity is intended as $P(\text{category} \mid \text{suffix})$.
issues.quote: We define diagnosticity as the strength with which a suffix spelling predicts lexical category. For a particular suffix, type diagnosticity is calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category. Diagnosticity is thus expressed as a ratio ranging from 0 to 1 . For example, -NIK is not diagnostic for adjectives (diagnosticity is 0 ), whereas -TUDE unambiguously signals a noun (diagnosticity is 1). A suffix like -IAN is present in nouns (magician), as well as in other categories (Amazonian), and so is not particularly diagnostic for nouns (type diagnosticity of 0.54 ).

issues.subcategory: Specificity token denominator in Method
issues.description: Specificity token denominator in Method: In the Method definition of token specificity, the denominator appears inconsistent with the construct and with the preceding type measure. Specificity is defined as choosing a spelling among alternative spellings of the same sound sequence within a category, but the token denominator is described as the frequency of words that contain the target spelling rather than all category words ending in the relevant sound sequence.
issues.quote: For a given lexical category, we then divided the number of words containing the suffix spelling (e.g. -LESS) by the total number of words of this lexical category with any spelling of the sound sequence. Like diagnosticity, specificity is expressed as a ratio ranging from 0 to 1 . Spellings with the specificity of 0 for a given category never go with this category (e.g. -IOUS never occurs in nouns), whereas the value of 1 indicates that the spelling has full specificity (e.g. when a noun ends in /ertə/, it must be spelled with -ATOR). Medium values of specificity indicate that there are multiple competing spellings, as with /ɪə/ (specificity of 0.48 , cf. cashier, engineer). A second measure of specificity, based on word tokens, was obtained by dividing the summed frequency of words ending in this phonological and orthographic sequence and falling into this category by the summed frequency of all words that contain the spelling and fall into this category.

issues.subcategory: The -ICAL specificity example is too absolute under the stated denominator
issues.description: The -ICAL specificity example is too absolute under the stated denominator: Under the method as written, the denominator for specificity is all words in the relevant category ending in the selected sound sequence, regardless of spelling. On that reading, adjectives such as “fickle” appear to be counterexamples to the absolute “must be spelled -ICAL” claim. If such words are excluded by the CELEX phonological coding or by a suffixal-case restriction, state that restriction here. Otherwise, replace the categorical wording with a graded claim about the analysed suffixal cases.
issues.quote: If a word contains the -ICAL spelling, it is almost certainly an adjective; and if the sound sequence / Ikəl/ is an adjective, then it must be spelled -ICAL.

issues.subcategory: Suffix-count arithmetic in Results
issues.description: Suffix-count arithmetic in Results: The robustness-check counts are internally inconsistent. The paper states that the inventory contains 154 suffixes, but excluding 64 would leave 90, not the 95 reported here. This should be reconciled so readers know which subset the reported means describe.
issues.quote: It is immediately apparent that a substantial number of suffixes have diagnosticity and specificity values of 1 . This means that these suffix spellings are always associated with a particular lexical category (diagnosticity) and that these suffix spellings are the only means of communicating a particular lexical category for a given word-final sound sequence (specificity). Is it possible that this very strong relationship between spelling and lexical category is due to the presence of suffixes in our sample that occur only rarely? In order to determine this, we excluded all suffixes that occur in fewer than 20 different words in the CELEX database, i.e. 64 suffixes (Baayen et al., 1993). For the remaining 95 suffixes, the mean diagnosticity and specificity values were virtually unchanged (type and token diagnosticity mean $=0.76$; type specificity mean $=0.83$, token specificity mean $=0.82$ ).

issues.subcategory: Means do not answer whether perfect associations are driven by rare suffixes
issues.description: Means do not answer whether perfect associations are driven by rare suffixes: The question is about suffixes with exact values of 1, but the check reports only post-exclusion means. Similar means can coexist with a large drop in the number of suffixes at ceiling. Report how many suffixes have diagnosticity 1, specificity 1, and both values 1 before and after the low-frequency exclusion. Otherwise the analysis only shows that the averages are stable.
issues.quote: Is it possible that this very strong relationship between spelling and lexical category is due to the presence of suffixes in our sample that occur only rarely? In order to determine this, we excluded all suffixes that occur in fewer than 20 different words in the CELEX database, i.e. 64 suffixes (Baayen et al., 1993). For the remaining 95 suffixes, the mean diagnosticity and specificity values were virtually unchanged (type and token diagnosticity mean $=0.76$; type specificity mean $=0.83$, token specificity mean $=0.82$ ).

issues.subcategory: The conclusion strengthens an either-or result into a both-and claim
issues.description: The conclusion strengthens an either-or result into a both-and claim: Earlier the Results section says that the majority are “either diagnostic or specific or both”. This conclusion states the stronger intersection claim, but no threshold or count is given for suffixes that are both diagnostic and specific. Define the cut-off and report the number satisfying each condition, or soften the sentence to “diagnostic, specific, or both”.
issues.quote: Our analyses demonstrate that the majority of written English derivational suffixes are diagnostic and specific for some lexical category.

issues.subcategory: Reversed feedforward mapping in transition
issues.description: Reversed feedforward mapping in transition: The transition reverses the mapping between constructs and tasks. Diagnosticity is defined as spelling-to-meaning consistency and should be linked to print-to-meaning tasks; specificity is defined as meaning-to-spelling consistency and should be linked to spelling production. The subsequent Experiments section uses this opposite, conceptually correct mapping.
issues.quote: In this paper, we focus solely on what is usually referred to as "feedforward" effects. That is, we hypothesise that diagnosticity, a measure of spelling-to-meaning consistency, would impact on tasks that involve the production of spelling, while specificity, a measure of meaning-to-spelling consistency, would impact on tasks involving the mapping of print to meaning (i.e. semantic categorisation, reading). That said, perception and production are intertwined processes, and one might expect "feedback" effects of diagnosticity and specificity as well (e.g. diagnosticity influencing the production of spelling; see Ziegler et al., 2008; Kessler et al., 2008, for similar findings in reading aloud). This is an issue that needs to be investigated in future studies using appropriate experimental designs (e.g. a two-by-two factorial manipulation).

issues.subcategory: 0.50 diagnosticity threshold represents chance, not "high" diagnosticity
issues.description: 0.50 diagnosticity threshold represents chance, not "high" diagnosticity: The description of all selected suffixes as having “high diagnosticity” is potentially misleading for suffixes near the lower bound. A value around 0.50 can indicate only a bare majority, and in a noun/adjective forced-choice setting may provide little discrimination if the remaining cases are mainly the other response category. The table and graded analyses mitigate this, but the threshold should not be interpreted as uniformly strong diagnosticity.
issues.quote: Twenty suffixes diagnostic for the noun or adjective category were selected (See Table 2). These suffixes all had a high diagnosticity, i.e. greater than or equal to 0.50 , and occurred in at least 20 different words.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 model omits item or suffix clustering
issues.description: Experiment 1 model omits item or suffix clustering: The Experiment 1 model appears under-specified for the structure of the data. Responses are clustered not only by participant but also by nonword item and by suffix, while the key predictors are properties of suffixes/items. Without item or suffix random effects, the trial-level model may overstate the precision of the condition and diagnosticity effects, especially for the graded diagnosticity analyses that depend on variation across only 20 suffixes, or 10 suffixes in the separate category-specific analyses.
issues.quote: We used generalised mixed modelling analysis from the Ime4 package in R (Bates et al., 2014) on 1,625 data points ( $11.7 \%$ of data points were missing due to timeouts or button presses that did not correspond to a response). The analysis considered the impact of suffix condition (adjective or noun suffix) on the binomial response (adjective or noun). We included a random intercept for subjects. This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response $\sim$ condition + ( 1 |subject), data, family $=$ "binomial").

issues.subcategory: Condition contrast does not establish the within-condition response pattern
issues.description: Condition contrast does not establish the within-condition response pattern: The reported coefficient compares response log-odds between suffix conditions. It does not by itself show that noun responses outnumbered adjective responses within the noun-diagnostic condition; that requires the intercept or estimated condition means. Add the fitted proportions for noun- and adjective-diagnostic suffixes, or rephrase the result as a between-condition contrast.
issues.quote: Results showed a main effect of suffix condition such that noun-diagnostic suffixes elicited more "noun" responses ( $B=-1.57, z=-4.224, p<0.0001$ ) than "adjective" responses.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 diagnosticity measure is unstable
issues.description: Experiment 1 diagnosticity measure is unstable: The written definition of type diagnosticity earlier in the paper appears inconsistent with the values used here. The concept, examples, and tables indicate a suffix-to-category measure, $P(\mathrm{category}\mid\mathrm{suffix})$, but the Method text describes dividing by the total number of words in the category, which would instead be $P(\mathrm{suffix}\mid\mathrm{category})$. Because Experiment 1 interprets diagnosticity as the strength with which a suffix predicts category, this operational definition should be made internally consistent.
issues.quote: Further analyses were conducted to investigate whether participants' knowledge of the suffix spellings' diagnosticity mirrors statistics of the writing system. That is, we asked whether participants were better at classifying nonwords that contain strongly diagnostic suffixes than those with a weaker diagnosticity. In order to investigate this statistically, we multiplied our diagnosticity measure by -1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes and substituted this measure in our model, in place of the condition variable.

issues.subcategory: Signed diagnosticity model conflates cue direction with cue strength
issues.description: Signed diagnosticity model conflates cue direction with cue strength: The signed predictor no longer measures diagnosticity strength alone. Adjective-diagnostic suffixes receive positive values and noun-diagnostic suffixes negative values, so moving from -0.8 to +0.8 changes both the strength and the cued category. The pooled slope may therefore mostly repeat the noun/adjective contrast already tested. Treat this model as a direction-of-cue check, and present the separate adjective- and noun-suffix models as the test of graded diagnosticity.
issues.quote: In order to investigate this statistically, we multiplied our diagnosticity measure by -1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes and substituted this measure in our model, in place of the condition variable. This analysis revealed a main effect of diagnosticity on response type: $B=0.87, z=4.13$, $p<0.0001$, such that more diagnostic suffixes were more likely to be ascribed to the category that they denote.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 switches diagnosticity and specificity terms
issues.description: Experiment 1 switches diagnosticity and specificity terms: The phrase “adjective-specific suffixes” appears in the middle of an Experiment 1 diagnosticity analysis. Because the paper treats diagnosticity and specificity as distinct technical constructs, this terminology is potentially misleading: the surrounding text, Table 2, and Figure 4 indicate that the adjective subset is being analysed for diagnosticity, not specificity.
issues.quote:
We performed this analysis separately for adjective- and noun- diagnostic suffixes to make sure that this effect was not due
to the sign-transformation of the diagnosticity variable, and observed the effect of diagnosticity on both adjective-specific suffixes ( $B=4.5, z=2.9, p<0.01$, i.e. highest absolute values for diagnosticity yield more adjective responses) and noun-diagnostic suffixes ( $B=-3.5, z=-2.05, p<0.05$, i.e. highest absolute values for diagnosticity yield more noun responses; see Figure 4).

issues.subcategory: Experiment 2 rationale conflicts with an earlier mapping
issues.description: Experiment 2 rationale conflicts with an earlier mapping: The Experiment 2 rationale is coherent in isolation, but it conflicts with the earlier feedforward-effects paragraph, which maps diagnosticity to spelling production and specificity to print-to-meaning tasks. Given the paper’s own definitions, Experiment 2 appropriately tests specificity; the earlier mapping appears reversed and creates avoidable confusion about the logic of the experimental sequence.
issues.quote: Experiment 2 was a spelling experiment designed to test adults' knowledge of the extent to which particular spellings are used to denote lexical category for a given sound sequence. We created nonwords with endings that could be spelled in more than one way. We presented these nonwords auditorily in meaningful contexts that biased participants to interpret them as nouns, adjectives, or verbs, and recorded participants' spellings of the nonwords. If participants have stored knowledge of the specificity of spellings for lexical category, then context should influence the spellings that they produce, such that they are congruent with the predicted category.

issues.subcategory: Unmatched stems confound spelling choices
issues.description: Unmatched stems confound spelling choices: The no-matching argument controls the suffix pronunciation, but not the preceding stem context. In Experiment 2, different stems were assigned to the congruent and incongruent conditions for each suffix, and the analyses appear to include only a subject random intercept. Because English spelling choices for word-final sequences can be influenced by preceding phonological or orthographic context, stem-specific biases could contribute to the observed condition effect unless item/stem variability is accounted for.
issues.quote: Note that no matching was required, because the same phonological sequence was used in the congruent and incongruent conditions. Thus, any effect could not be attributed to the properties of the phonological sequence or its possible spellings: for instance, had it been the spelling frequency that influenced participants' performance, we would observe no difference between the conditions at all (i.e., the most frequent spelling would be used regardless of the predicted lexical category).

issues.subcategory: The matching claim overstates what holding the suffix pronunciation controls
issues.description: The matching claim overstates what holding the suffix pronunciation controls: Holding the suffix pronunciation constant is a useful control, but it does not make matching unnecessary for the whole nonword. The stems differ across trials, and stem-final phonology or orthography can make one spelling of an ending more natural than another. The claim that “any effect” cannot be attributed to properties of the phonological sequence or possible spellings is therefore too broad. State more narrowly that the ending pronunciation was controlled, while stem-level influences were handled by random assignment or should be checked.
issues.quote: Note that no matching was required, because the same phonological sequence was used in the congruent and incongruent conditions. Thus, any effect could not be attributed to the properties of the phonological sequence or its possible spellings: for instance, had it been the spelling frequency that influenced participants' performance, we would observe no difference between the conditions at all (i.e., the most frequent spelling would be used regardless of the predicted lexical category).

issues.subcategory: Confound between items and conditions in Exp 2
issues.description: Confound between items and conditions in Exp 2: Experiment 2 seems to have specific nonwords nested within congruency condition, while the reported analysis is described as identical to Experiment 1 and therefore appears to include only a subject random intercept. Without counterbalancing or item/suffix random effects, the condition effect may be anti-conservative because item-level variation is not modelled.
issues.quote:
Each participant heard six nonwords containing each suffix: three times in a context congruent with the target spelling of the suffix, and three times in a context incongruent with it. For instance, three different /əs/-nonwords were embedded in sentences where they functioned as adjectives (congruent context where the target spelling -OUS is expected), and three different/əs/-nonwords were embedded in sentences where they functioned as nouns (any other spelling is expected but not-OUS). See Appendix C for the complete list of stimulus materials.

Table 4 about here

Each subject saw all 66 sentences.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 2 Results: random-effects structure is unclear
issues.description: Experiment 2 Results: random-effects structure is unclear: The Experiment 2 binomial model appears to inherit only the subject random intercept from Experiment 1. Because observations are clustered by suffix and by stimulus sentence/nonword, the reported congruency effect may overstate precision and does not make clear whether the inference generalises beyond the sampled suffixes and items.
issues.quote: Suffix spellings were manually extracted from whole nonword spellings ( 1,914 analysable data points). The dependent variable was binary and coded whether the actual spelling was the target spelling for this suffix or not (see Table 3 for the list of target spellings associated with spoken endings). The analysis considered the impact of context condition (congruent or incongruent context) on the binomial response (target spelling or other spelling). The analyses were otherwise identical to those in Experiment 1.

issues.subcategory: Missing item random effects in specificity analysis
issues.description: Missing item random effects in specificity analysis: The specificity analysis appears to use the same subject-only random-effects structure as Experiment 1. Because specificity is a suffix-level predictor with only eleven target suffixes, the main effect of specificity and the specificity-by-condition interaction may have anti-conservative standard errors unless suffix/item clustering is modelled or otherwise accounted for.
issues.quote: The analysis considered the impact of context condition (congruent or incongruent context) on the binomial response (target spelling or other spelling). The analyses were otherwise identical to those in Experiment 1. Results were such that the target spelling was less frequent in the incongruent context condition

issues.subcategory: Specificity interaction tests a different question from the one stated
issues.description: Specificity interaction tests a different question from the one stated: The stated moderation question asks whether the congruent-minus-incongruent effect is larger for spellings with higher specificity. For that test, specificity should be a fixed property of the target spelling across conditions. The parenthetical says the fitted value changes with context, so the model instead asks whether target-spelling use tracks the spelling's specificity for the currently cued category. Either revise the hypothesis to match that model, or refit the analysis with target-spelling specificity held constant across congruent and incongruent trials.
issues.quote: In order to investigate this hypothesis, we added the graded specificity metric for the target spelling to the linear model (values were different in different contexts because specificity of spellings was estimated relative to different categories), as well as its interaction with the condition variable.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent token-analysis statistic in Experiment 2
issues.description: Inconsistent token-analysis statistic in Experiment 2: The token-analysis result in Experiment 2 appears internally inconsistent: a reported statistic with magnitude $z=0.60$ cannot correspond to $p<0.01$ under the usual Wald normal approximation. This looks like a reporting error in either the statistic or the $p$ value.
issues.quote: As predicted, the interaction between specificity and condition was significant, such that the target spelling became used more often in the congruent condition than in the incongruent condition as its specificity increased ( $B=1.9, z=2.8, p<0.01$; for the token analyses $-z=0.60, p<0.01$ ); there was no effect of specificity in the incongruent condition. These results are visualised in Figure 6.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 3 fillers are not clearly verb-diagnostic
issues.description: Experiment 3 fillers are not clearly verb-diagnostic: Experiment 3’s filler description appears internally inconsistent: the fillers are introduced as having suffix spellings diagnostic for verbs, but the next sentence says most verb suffixes have diagnosticity below 0.5, and Appendix A indicates that several listed suffixes are more noun- than verb-associated. Since the fillers were intended to balance sentence contexts rather than enter the main analyses, this may not affect the primary results, but the passage should distinguish syntactic-context balance from verb-diagnostic suffix cues.
issues.quote: Stimuli. Eighty experimental nonwords with suffix spellings diagnostic for adjectives ( 10 suffixes) or nouns ( 10 suffixes) were selected from Experiment 1. Forty filler nonwords whose suffix spellings were diagnostic for verbs were added so that sentence contexts would be balanced across all three lexical categories. These filler nonwords were not analysed, because the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category (i.e. diagnosticity is less than 0.5 ). The ten verb suffixes we used as fillers were -ate, -ade, -eer, -le, -yse, -ide, -our, -ice, -ure, -art.

issues.subcategory: Pretarget word-count imbalance may affect key eye measures
issues.description: Pretarget word-count imbalance may affect key eye measures: The significant pre-target word-count imbalance is a potential confound for go-past time and regressions-out, because these measures can include or be triggered by regressions into the pre-target region. Although pre-target letters were matched and the difference is small, the analysis as described does not show that the congruency effects survive controlling for pre-target word count or related sentence-frame properties.
issues.quote: Sentence parts preceding targets were matched across conditions on the number of letters (congruent: 30.48 letters on average, incongruent: 31.70 letters, $p>0.3$ ). Note that the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, $\mathrm{t}(64)=2.07, \mathrm{p}<0.05$ ). Post-target contexts were matched on the number of letters ( 25.02 vs 26.33 , respectively, $\mathrm{p}>0.05$ ) and the number of words ( 4.38 vs 4.56 , respectively, $\mathrm{p}>0.05$ ). Pretarget words were always at least five characters long (with no difference across conditions: $7.33 \mathrm{vs} 7.15, \mathrm{p}>0.6$ ), to reduce the likelihood of these words being skipped.

issues.subcategory: Impossible degrees of freedom in stimulus matching
issues.description: Impossible degrees of freedom in stimulus matching: The reported $t(64)$ for the pre-target word-count matching test is ambiguous. If this was a conventional equal-variance item test over the 80 analysed targets, the expected degrees of freedom would be 78, or 118 if all 120 sentences were included. However, $df=64$ could arise from a Welch test, rounding, or a different subset, so the item set and test used need to be specified for readers to verify that the matching applies to the Experiment 3 materials.
issues.quote: Sentence parts preceding targets were matched across conditions on the number of letters (congruent: 30.48 letters on average, incongruent: 31.70 letters, $p>0.3$ ). Note that the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, $\mathrm{t}(64)=2.07, \mathrm{p}<0.05$ ).

issues.subcategory: Anomalous viewing distance
issues.description: Anomalous viewing distance: The reported 140 cm viewing distance seems difficult to reconcile with the stated 14pt Courier display and horizontal character width of $0.3^\circ$. At 140 cm, $0.3^\circ$ per character would require unusually large characters or display scaling, but the paper reports only pixel resolution rather than the monitor’s physical size; if 140 cm is not a typographical error, the display geometry needs to be accounted for.
issues.quote: Participants were seated at a viewing distance of 140 cm , with this position maintained with a table-mounted head and chin rest. The eye-tracking task was conducted on an LED monitor

issues.subcategory: Unreported pre-sentence trial exclusions in Procedure
issues.description: Unreported pre-sentence trial exclusions in Procedure: The Procedure describes a pre-sentence fixation-trigger failure that ended and discarded a trial, but the Results only report that $4\%$ of trials were discarded after the eye-tracking cleaning and visual-inspection checks. It is therefore unclear whether fixation-trigger failures are included in that $4\%$ and how many trials, if any, were lost before sentence display.
issues.quote: A drift-correction point was displayed at the beginning of every trial, positioned at the location of the sentence onset. An additional check on recording accuracy was performed by displaying a gaze-contingent square of 2.5 characters' width ( 0.80 ) in this same location, following completion of the drift correction. Participants were required to fixate this square for at least 40 ms to trigger the onset of the sentence. If a participant failed to do this, the trial was ended and discarded from further analysis, and the calibration procedure was repeated before the next trial was presented.

issues.subcategory: Comprehension accuracy is reported on the wrong scale
issues.description: Comprehension accuracy is reported on the wrong scale: A literal reading gives accuracy below 1%, which would indicate failed comprehension. The range looks like proportions, not percentages. Report this as “0.86 (86%; range 0.66–0.98)” or as “86% (range 66%–98%)” so the data-quality check is clear.
issues.quote: Average accuracy on comprehension trials was $0.86 \%$ (ranging from $0.66 \%$ to $0.98 \%$ ).

issues.subcategory: Regressions-in are not an initial lexical-processing measure
issues.description: Regressions-in are not an initial lexical-processing measure: This sentence sweeps regressions-in into the early-processing group, but the paper defines regressions-in as the target receiving a regression from later parts of the sentence. That is a later reinspection measure, not an initial lexical measure like first fixation duration or first-run dwell time. Separate the null effects on skipping/first-pass measures from the null effect on regressions-in.
issues.quote: We did not find any significant effect of congruency on any of the other measures reported, all of which are thought to reflect initial lexical processing (e.g. Rayner \& Liversedge, 2011).

issues.subcategory: Likelihood-ratio test degrees of freedom do not match the wording
issues.description: Likelihood-ratio test degrees of freedom do not match the wording: If only a single diagnosticity-by-congruency interaction term was added, the likelihood-ratio test would normally have 1 degree of freedom. The reported Chi(2) implies that two fixed-effect terms were added, most likely diagnosticity plus the interaction. The sentence should say so; otherwise the model comparison is not reproducible from the text.
issues.quote: The fit of regressions-out model improved significantly when the interaction was added: Chi $(2)=14.37, \mathrm{p}<0.001$.

issues.subcategory: Simple slopes are labelled as a main effect
issues.description: Simple slopes are labelled as a main effect: These are condition-specific simple slopes, not a single main effect of diagnosticity. The two estimates differ by about 0.36, which matches the reported interaction coefficient of 0.37 up to rounding. Label these as simple-slope analyses, and reserve “main effect” for a model coefficient under a stated contrast coding.
issues.quote: First, there was a main effect of diagnosticity: the probability of regressing to previous regions of the sentence decreased as diagnosticity increased in the congruent condition ( $B=-0.15, z=-2.31, p<0.05$ ), and increased as diagnosticity increased in the incongruent condition (marginal significance, $\mathrm{B}=0.21, \mathrm{z}=1.8, \mathrm{p}=0.08$ ).

issues.subcategory: Go-past slowing is treated as caused by regressions without a mediation test
issues.description: Go-past slowing is treated as caused by regressions without a mediation test: The analyses show a congruency effect on go-past time and a separate effect on regressions-out. They do not show that regressions statistically explain the go-past effect. Since go-past time already includes time spent after regressive movements until the eyes move past the target, the two measures are related by definition. A safer phrasing is that both measures are consistent with integration difficulty in incongruent contexts.
issues.quote: Experiment 3 demonstrated that adults are slower to progress past the target nonword whose spelling is incongruent with the predicted lexical category. This is likely due to the fact that such situations cause participants to regress to earlier regions of the sentence.

issues.subcategory: Diagnosticity effects are stated more broadly than the simple slopes support
issues.description: Diagnosticity effects are stated more broadly than the simple slopes support: The regression-out analysis supports an interaction, but the go-past simple slopes are weaker: no reliable diagnosticity effect in the congruent condition and only a trend in the incongruent condition. The wording makes facilitation and disruption sound established across reading measures. Narrow the claim to say that diagnosticity modulated some integration measures, with the clearest evidence in regressions-out.
issues.quote: Further, the strength of the relationship between suffix spelling and lexical category modulates this integration difficulty. Reading is facilitated when suffix spellings that are strongly diagnostic of a particular lexical category are used in contexts that are congruent with that category; conversely, reading is disrupted when such spellings are used in contexts that are incongruent with that category.

issues.subcategory: Cross-orthographic claim in General Discussion needs more precision
issues.description: Cross-orthographic claim in General Discussion needs more precision: In the General Discussion, the text transitions from stating that 'fractionation could not occur in a spelling-sound transparent writing system' to the claim that diagnosticity and specificity 'must manifest, in one way or another, in other orthographies.' It is slightly unclear how specificity—which is operationalised earlier as depending on the existence of multiple spellings for a shared sound sequence—would meaningfully manifest in a transparent orthography where such competing spellings are absent. Clarifying what form specificity might take in such systems, or whether the claim is restricted to opaque orthographies, would sharpen this theoretical point.
issues.quote:
This fractionation could not occur in a spelling-sound transparent writing system. Second, it suggests that the written signal conveys more disambiguating information than the spoken signal in these cases. We believe that this may have important implications for our understanding of skilled reading (see Rastle, 2017).

It is our view that diagnosticity and specificity are characteristic not of the English writing system exclusively but rather reflect general cognitive principles and thus must manifest, in one way or another, in other orthographies. Further research is needed, however, to test this conjecture. We chose English as a starting point for this work, because its
spelling evolved under minimal environmental constraints (unlike French and Italian whose development was regulated by language academies, see Berg and Aronoff, 2017).

issues.subcategory: Contradiction regarding transparent orthographies
issues.description: Contradiction regarding transparent orthographies: The claim in the General Discussion that diagnosticity and specificity 'must manifest, in one way or another, in other orthographies' sits in slight tension with the immediately preceding point that 'fractionation could not occur in a spelling-sound transparent writing system.' Since a perfectly transparent writing system mathematically cannot exhibit orthography-specific diagnosticity and specificity that diverges from its phonology, it would be helpful to clarify the exact scope of this cross-linguistic claim. For example, the paper could briefly specify whether this principle applies primarily to other opaque orthographies, or whether these cognitive pressures pattern differently (e.g., via spoken language) in transparent ones.
issues.quote: It is our view that diagnosticity and specificity are characteristic not of the English writing system exclusively but rather reflect general cognitive principles and thus must manifest, in one way or another, in other orthographies.

issues.subcategory: Invalid statistical test for mean entropy differences
issues.description: Invalid statistical test for mean entropy differences: The statistical test used for the entropy comparison does not directly test the substantive hypothesis. A regression slope for $H_{\mathrm{spelling}}$ on $H_{\mathrm{phonology}}$ measures association and scale change; unless the intercept is constrained and justified, testing whether the slope differs from 1 is not equivalent to testing whether $H_{\mathrm{spelling}}$ is systematically lower than $H_{\mathrm{phonology}}$. The reported mean difference is small, so the inference that spelling provides significantly more category information is not established by the slope test as described.
issues.quote: We then examined the slope of the regression equation $\operatorname{Im}$ (Hspelling $\sim$ Hphonology). There are three possible outcomes from this analysis. A slope of 1 indicates that suffix pronunciations and their spellings provide the same degree of information about lexical category; a slope greater than 1 indicates that phonology is more predictive of category compared to spelling; and a slope less than 1 would support our conjecture that spelling is more predictive of category compared to phonology.

issues.subcategory: Scalar diagnosticity is unclear in frequency analysis
issues.description: Scalar diagnosticity is unclear in frequency analysis: There seems to be an issue with the frequency analysis because diagnosticity is treated as a single scalar value per suffix, whereas the paper otherwise reports category-specific values for adjectives, nouns, and verbs. It is not clear whether the correlation uses the maximum diagnosticity across categories, the dominant category’s value, or another summary; this also makes the exclusion rule for low-diagnosticity suffixes difficult to reconstruct.
issues.quote:
Why are some suffixes more diagnostic than others?
Preliminary analyses we conducted to understanding why some morphemes are diagnostic, while others are not. For this analysis, we removed seven suffixes with diagnosticity below 0.35 , because these are indicative of lexical categories we have not considered in this paper (e.g. -WISE, -TEEN). Next, we tested if diagnosticity is a property of more frequent suffixes by correlating type frequency and type-based diagnosticity. Surprisingly, the correlation was negative, i.e. $-0.24, \mathrm{p}<0.01$, but this was entirely due to suffixes with diagnosticity of 1 . There are 40 such suffixes, and they can be highly frequent (e.g. -ISM), as well as very infrequent (e.g. -NIK, -DROME). In fact, all extremely infrequent suffixes are diagnostic; that is, they appear in a very small number of words of one lexical category, and do not tolerate any exceptions, which might mean that such infrequent suffixes are not retained in language unless they are diagnostic. Once we remove these 40 suffixes, a positive correlation is observed ( $0.23, p<0.05$ ), meaning that highly diagnostic suffixes tend to be those that occur in many words.

issues.subcategory: Unjustified data exclusion reversing correlation
issues.description: Unjustified data exclusion reversing correlation: The positive frequency–diagnosticity claim is based on a subset that excludes the 40 suffixes with diagnosticity of 1. Since the full analysis first shows a negative correlation driven by rare perfectly diagnostic suffixes, the conclusion that highly diagnostic suffixes tend to occur in many words is only justified for the non-ceiling subset and is too broad if read as a general statement about all suffixes.

issues.subcategory: The rare-suffix retention interpretation can arise from sparse denominators
issues.description: The rare-suffix retention interpretation can arise from sparse denominators: The retention interpretation is stronger than the calculation warrants. With very small type counts, type diagnosticity is highly discretised: a suffix with one observed type in one category has diagnosticity 1 by construction, and a suffix with two observed types can only take coarse values such as 1/2 or 2/2. These ceiling cases may reflect sparse counts rather than a language-level pressure against retaining non-diagnostic rare suffixes. Present this as a descriptive pattern unless a separate diachronic or sampling analysis is added.

issues.subcategory: Extreme data loss invalidating specificity claim
issues.description: Extreme data loss invalidating specificity claim: The specificity–frequency correlation is computed after excluding all suffixes with specificity of 1, leaving 36 type items and 26 token items. Because many suffixes appear to be at this ceiling, the resulting positive relationship should be interpreted as applying only to the non-ceiling subset; stated more generally, it risks misrepresenting a distribution in which a large proportion of suffixes are already perfectly specific.

issues.subcategory: Orthographic-ending comparison needs more support
issues.description: Orthographic-ending comparison needs more support: The orthographic-ending comparison is difficult to evaluate from the information given here. Because Figure 9 is used to distinguish morphological suffixes from lower-level word-final orthographic cues, it would be important to know how overlapping final strings were counted, what exactly qualified as “not part of existing suffixes”, and whether diagnosticity and frequency for these endings were computed in the same type/token terms used for suffixes.
issues.quote: Our view is that there are fundamental differences between low-level orthographic and morphological cues, in terms of the degree of precision with which the latter are encoded in written language, and also in terms of their distributional properties. To illustrate some distributional differences, suffixes are a closed class of units, whereas the number of orthographic units is a magnitude larger and depends on the definition that one adopts. For example, do orthographic units include written word bodies (e.g. -EAL; Arcuili and Cupples, 2006), or one-letter/phoneme units (e.g. Onnis and Christiansen, 2008; see discussion in Ktori et al., 2017). Figure 9 plots the distributions of suffixes and orthographic endings (all one, two, three, four, and five letter endings that are not part of existing suffixes). Not only there are fewer suffixes than other endings, but the former are also higher in diagnosticity and frequency (most diagnostic suffixes are highly frequent, whereas highly diagnostic endings are rare). The majority of non-suffix endings are indicative of the noun category ( $88 \%$ ), with the remaining $11 \%$ pointing to verbs. Only two endings (-UNG and -LETE) are strongly associated with the adjective category. On the other hand, suffixes allow for discriminating nouns ( $65 \%$ ) and adjectives $(30 \%)$. Finally, suffixes' combinatorial nature permits a substantial degree of productivity that is absent for non-morphemic sequences.

issues.subcategory: Internal contradiction regarding suffix frequency
issues.description: Internal contradiction regarding suffix frequency: The phrase “most diagnostic suffixes are highly frequent” is potentially ambiguous in light of the preceding analysis, which notes that the suffixes with diagnosticity of 1 include very infrequent items. If Figure 9 is referring to a different threshold, subset, or visual pattern than the earlier correlation analysis, that scope is not clear from the text.

If the adjective cases are a rounded residual, avoid “remaining”. A clearer version would give approximate noun, verb, and adjective figures separately.

issues.subcategory: The -AL conclusion slightly outruns the evidence
issues.description: The -AL conclusion slightly outruns the evidence: The final claim about readers using -AL in “vorpal” is somewhat stronger than the direct evidence for that specific suffix. The paper provides a corpus-level association between -AL and adjective status, and a broader demonstration that readers use diagnostic suffix spellings, but -AL is also described as relatively ambiguous and was not one of the analysed print-to-meaning suffixes in Experiments 1 and 3.
issues.quote: In summary, we have provided a new way to think about English writing, in which one consequence of the apparent disorder of spelling-sound information is order in the spelling-meaning mapping. We have shown that literate adults are sensitive to these regularities between spelling and meaning, and that their long-term knowledge mirrors the strength of these regularities in the writing system. These conclusions suggest that reading the poem Jabberwocky (Carroll, 1871/1983) provides information about meaning that is not present when listening to the poem. Carroll's (1871/1983) choice of the spelling "vorpal" to describe the blade (as opposed to "vorple") was unlikely to be random, even if he didn't know that to be the case. Further, our research suggests that readers take advantage of the relationship between spelling -AL and adjective status to assist their interpretation of this part of the poem. One interesting pathway for future research will be to chart how these regularities emerged through spelling changes in the development of English writing.

**Construct alignment and formal definitions**

The central constructs of diagnosticity and specificity provide an intriguing way to look at meaning in orthography. Establishing formal statements of each conditional probability early on would help track these concepts systematically across the sections. In the Method section, diagnosticity is introduced conceptually as spelling predicting lexical category, implying $P(\text{category} | \text{spelling})$. However, the corresponding type formula divides by "the total number of words falling into this category", mapping instead onto $P(\text{spelling} | \text{category})$. The token formula and the values in Table 2 appear to revert to the initial predicting-category construct. Similarly, the token definition of specificity uses a denominator comprising "all words that contain the spelling and fall into this category", which departs from the stated construct of comparing competing spellings for the same sound sequence and category. There is also an apparent reversal of the task predictions for these two constructs within the "feedforward effects" paragraph, before the original predictions are restored in the Experiments section. The computational analysis argues that robust diagnosticity and specificity are ubiquitous across English derivational suffixes. Unpacking the extraction procedure used on the CELEX database would lend weight to this corpus-scale claim. The methodology admits genuine and pseudo-suffixed words when the residual string matches a CELEX stem, but readers might wonder how overlapping or nested suffixes (such as -AL/-IAL/-ICAL and -TION/-ATION) are resolved. Furthermore, how are false-positive pseudo-suffixes constrained, and what role do non-noun/adjective/verb categories play in the resulting distributions? Appendix A includes suffix entries like +LY, +ALLY, +SELF, +WISE, single-letter endings, and suffixes exhibiting zero values across analysed categories. Reproducible extraction algorithms paired with sensitivity analyses—perhaps excluding pseudo-suffixed candidates or nested suffixes—would definitively demonstrate that the observed patterns reflect general English morphology rather than specific parsing rules.

The experiments generate extremely rich trial-level data. The current mixed-effects architecture models this with random intercepts tailored solely for participants, despite inferences extending to suffixes, stems, sentence contexts, and spelling alternatives. This becomes particularly consequential during the graded analyses where diagnosticity is estimated over 20 suffixes and specificity over 11 target spellings, as treating repeated observations from a given suffix as statistically independent leaves the models exposed to item-level idiosyncrasies. Limiting claims regarding "access to meaning" strictly to contextual integration stages would align the interpretation with the available eye-tracking evidence. Interpreting the null early eye-movement effects as proof that category information only becomes influential after initial lexical processing assumes an absence of early sensitivity; these null effects may instead emerge from task power limitations or unfamiliar nonword-processing dynamics.

The paper builds toward a fascinating argument that English spelling has evolved to be functional, transmitting meaningful category information in exchange for spelling-sound inconsistency.
